micro_skills.subtopic: Real Numbers and the Real Line
micro_skills.micro_skill: Solving linear inequalities
definitions: An inequality is solved using the same operations as an equation, EXCEPT that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality.

theorems.name: Rules for Inequalities
theorems.statement: For real numbers a, b, c: (1) a<b => a+c<b+c; (2) a<b => a-c<b-c; (3) a<b and c>0 => ac<bc; (4) a<b and c<0 => ac>bc; (5) a>0 => 1/a>0; (6) 0<a<b => 1/b<1/a.
conditions: Rules 1-4 and 6 (for a>0) also hold with <=, >=
Rule 4 is the source of the 'flip the inequality' rule when multiplying/dividing by a negative

formulas: solution sets are written as intervals, e.g. (4, infinity)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a linear inequality of the form ax+b (comparison) cx+d and express the solution as an interval
question_archetypes.example: Solve 2x-1 > x+3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A single inequality symbol with x appearing only to the first power on both sides
method_plan: Collect all x-terms on one side by adding/subtracting (does not affect direction)
Collect constants on the other side
Divide by the coefficient of x, flipping the inequality if that coefficient is negative
Write the answer as an interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct collection of x-terms
M1: correct collection of constants
A1: correct final inequality with correct direction
A1: solution expressed as a correct interval

common_errors.description: Arithmetic slip when moving terms across the inequality
Sign error combining like terms
Leaving the answer as an inequality without converting to interval notation when asked

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a linear inequality that requires dividing by a negative coefficient
question_archetypes.example: Solve 3-2x <= 9
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: After isolating the x-term, the coefficient of x is negative
method_plan: Isolate the term containing x
Divide both sides by the (negative) coefficient of x
Reverse the inequality symbol because the divisor is negative
Write the solution as an interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly isolates the x-term
A1: correctly divides by the negative coefficient
A1: correctly reverses the inequality direction
A1: correct interval notation

common_errors.description: Forgetting to flip the inequality when dividing/multiplying by a negative number
Sign error isolating the x-term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a compound (double) linear inequality of the form k1 < expr < k2
question_archetypes.example: Solve -1 <= 2x+3 < 7
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two inequality symbols sandwiching a single linear expression
method_plan: Apply the same operation to all three parts simultaneously
Subtract the constant term from all three parts
Divide all three parts by the coefficient of x, flipping both symbols if it is negative
Write the solution as a single interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: operates on all three parts consistently
A1: correct intermediate compound inequality
A1: correct final interval including correct open/closed endpoints

common_errors.description: Only performing the operation on two of the three parts
Mixing up which endpoint is open vs closed from the original <= vs <

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a linear inequality with x-terms and fractions on both sides
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Fractions with constant (sign-known) denominators appear alongside x on both sides
method_plan: Multiply through by the least common denominator (a known positive constant, so direction is unchanged)
Expand and collect x-terms on one side, constants on the other
Divide by the coefficient of x, flipping if negative
State the solution as an interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct clearing of denominators
M1: correct expansion/collection
A1: correct final inequality and interval

common_errors.description: Distributing incorrectly when multiplying a bracketed expression by the LCD
Forgetting that multiplying by a negative denominator (if one appeared) would require flipping

micro_skills.subtopic: Real Numbers and the Real Line
micro_skills.micro_skill: Sign-chart method for rational and quadratic inequalities
definitions: To solve a nonlinear inequality, move everything to one side to compare a single expression to 0, factor/combine into one fraction, locate the critical points (zeros and points of discontinuity), and use a sign chart across the intervals they create.
formulas: P(x)/Q(x) <=> 0 solved via sign chart with critical points where P=0 or Q=0

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a quadratic inequality by factoring and reading the sign between the roots
question_archetypes.example: Solve x^2 - 5x + 6 < 0
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A polynomial inequality of degree 2 that is compared to 0, factorable into two linear factors
method_plan: Move all terms to one side so the other side is 0
Factor the quadratic
Find the roots (critical points)
Build a sign chart using a test point in each interval
Select the interval(s) matching the required sign
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct factoring
M1: correct sign chart with all intervals tested
A1: correct interval matching the required inequality direction

common_errors.description: Factoring error (wrong pair of roots)
Assuming the product is negative outside the roots instead of between them (sign pattern confusion)
Using strict vs non-strict boundary incorrectly (< vs <=)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a rational inequality of the form expr <= k (or >=, <, >) by moving everything to one side into a single fraction before sign-charting
question_archetypes.example: Solve 2/(x-1) <= 5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The variable appears in a denominator, and the inequality is not already compared to 0
method_plan: Subtract the right-hand side from both sides so the inequality is compared to 0
Combine into a single fraction over a common denominator
Identify critical points: zeros of the numerator and zeros of the denominator (denominator zeros are always excluded)
Build a sign chart across the resulting intervals
Select the interval(s) with the correct sign, excluding points where the denominator is 0
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly moves everything to one side (does NOT cross-multiply by an expression of unknown sign)
M1: correctly combines into a single fraction
M1: correct sign chart with all critical points identified
A1: correct final interval with denominator zero properly excluded

common_errors.description: Cross-multiplying by (x-1) without knowing its sign, silently assuming it's positive
Forgetting to exclude the point where the denominator is zero even though it looks like it should be included from the inequality direction
Sign error combining the fraction (e.g. mis-expanding -5(x-1))

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a rational/polynomial inequality whose sign chart involves a repeated factor (which never changes sign) or three or more critical points
question_archetypes.answer: x=2, or -1<=x<3, or x>3; i.e. {2} U [-1,3) U (3, infinity)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A squared (or even-power) factor appears in the numerator or denominator alongside other simple factors
method_plan: Identify all critical points from every factor
Note that an even-power factor does not change sign at its root (it only touches zero there)
Build the sign chart tracking each factor's sign separately, then multiply
Decide whether critical points from the numerator are included (if the inequality is non-strict) and always exclude denominator zeros
Write the final solution set, including isolated points where the expression equals zero if the inequality is non-strict
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of all critical points
M1: correctly treats the even-power factor as sign-nonnegative everywhere
A1: correct combined sign chart
A1: correct solution set including isolated equality points and excluded denominator zero

common_errors.description: Treating a squared factor as if it changes sign like a simple linear factor
Forgetting to check whether the boundary point should be included (non-strict) or excluded (denominator zero)
Writing the union of intervals with incorrect notation, e.g. omitting an isolated point

micro_skills.subtopic: Real Numbers and the Real Line
micro_skills.micro_skill: Solving absolute value equations
definitions: |x| = x if x>=0 and |x| = -x if x<0, equivalently |x| = sqrt(x^2). Solving |expr| = k (k>=0) splits into the two cases expr = k and expr = -k.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve |ax+b| = k for a constant k>=0
question_archetypes.example: Solve |2x+3| = 7
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Absolute value bars around a linear expression set equal to a nonnegative constant
method_plan: Split into two cases: ax+b = k and ax+b = -k
Solve each linear equation
State both solutions
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly splits into two cases
A1: correct solution to case 1
A1: correct solution to case 2

common_errors.description: Only solving one of the two cases
Sign error solving one of the linear equations

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve |expr1| = |expr2| where both sides involve x
question_archetypes.example: Solve |3x-1| = |x+5|
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Absolute value expressions appear on both sides of the equation
method_plan: Use |A|=|B| iff A=B or A=-B
Solve A=B
Solve A=-B
State both solutions (no domain restriction needed since both sides were already nonnegative by construction)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly splits into A=B and A=-B
A1: correct solution from each case

common_errors.description: Squaring both sides unnecessarily and mishandling the resulting expansion
Only finding one of the two solutions

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve |expr| = (expression involving x that could be negative), requiring a check for extraneous roots
question_archetypes.example: Solve |x-3| = 2x
question_archetypes.answer: x = 1 (x=-3 is rejected as extraneous since RHS must be >= 0)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The right-hand side of |expr|=RHS contains the variable, so its sign is not guaranteed
method_plan: Note the right-hand side must be >= 0 for any solution to be valid (since the left side is an absolute value)
Split into the two cases expr = RHS and expr = -RHS
Solve each case
Check each candidate solution against the original equation (reject extraneous ones)
full_mark_rubric: M1: recognizes the nonnegativity requirement on the RHS
M1: correctly splits and solves both cases
A1: correctly checks and rejects the extraneous solution

common_errors.description: Failing to check solutions back in the original equation, keeping an extraneous root
Sign error in one of the two split equations

micro_skills.subtopic: Real Numbers and the Real Line
micro_skills.micro_skill: Solving absolute value inequalities and using the triangle inequality
definitions: Distance interpretation: |x-y| is the distance from x to y on the number line.
For D>0: |x-a|<D iff a-D<x<a+D (a bounded interval); |x-a|>D iff x<a-D or x>a+D (two rays).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve |ax+b| <= D (or <) and give the solution as a bounded interval
question_archetypes.example: Solve |3x-2| <= 1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Absolute value of a linear expression is bounded above by a positive constant
method_plan: Rewrite as the compound inequality -D <= ax+b <= D
Solve the compound inequality for x
State the answer as a closed (or open, matching strictness) bounded interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrites as compound inequality
A1: correctly isolates x across all three parts
A1: correct interval with matching open/closed endpoints

common_errors.description: Using the 'greater than' pattern (two disjoint rays) instead of the bounded-interval pattern
Wrong endpoint inclusivity (using < instead of <=)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve |ax+b| >= D (or >) and give the solution as a union of two rays
question_archetypes.example: Solve |2x+3| >= 7
question_archetypes.answer: x <= -5 or x >= 2, i.e. (-infinity,-5] U [2, infinity)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Absolute value of a linear expression is bounded below by a positive constant
method_plan: Split into ax+b >= D or ax+b <= -D
Solve each linear inequality separately
Combine with 'or' as a union of two intervals
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly splits into the two-ray pattern
A1: correct solution of each branch
A1: correctly written union

common_errors.description: Using the compound (bounded interval) pattern meant for '<' instead of the two-ray pattern for '>'
Sign error flipping the second branch's inequality

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve an absolute value inequality whose argument is nonlinear, requiring conversion to a compound inequality and then a sign chart / quadratic solve
question_archetypes.example: Solve |x^2-4| < 3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The expression inside the absolute value bars is quadratic (or otherwise nonlinear) rather than linear
method_plan: Convert to the compound inequality -3 < x^2-4 < 3
Split into two separate quadratic inequalities: x^2-4 < 3 and x^2-4 > -3
Solve each quadratic inequality (factor or use the quadratic formula, then sign chart)
Intersect the two solution sets
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly converts to compound inequality
M1: correctly solves each of the two resulting quadratic inequalities
A1: correctly intersects the two solution sets into the final interval(s)

common_errors.description: Treating the nonlinear argument the same as the linear case without solving two separate quadratic inequalities
Forgetting to intersect (rather than union) the two resulting solution sets
Errors solving the quadratic inequalities themselves

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the triangle inequality to bound an expression, typically as a step in an epsilon-delta or estimation argument
question_archetypes.example: Given |x-2|<1, show |x^2-4| < 5|x-2| by bounding |x+2|
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks to bound |f(x)-L| in terms of |x-a|, typically inside a proof rather than asking for a numeric solution set
method_plan: Factor the target expression to isolate |x-a| as one factor
Use the given restriction on |x-a| (e.g. assume it's less than 1) to bound the remaining factor
Combine the bound on the remaining factor with the |x-a| factor to get the final estimate
State the resulting inequality clearly
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly factors to isolate |x-a|
M1: correctly uses the auxiliary restriction to bound the other factor
A1: correct final combined bound, clearly justified

common_errors.description: Trying to bound the whole expression at once instead of factoring out |x-a| first
Using an unjustified auxiliary restriction (not stating why delta<=1 was assumed)
Not clearly connecting the bound back to the original quantity being estimated

micro_skills.micro_skill: Distance and midpoint formulas
definitions: For P1(x1,y1) and P2(x2,y2): Delta x = x2-x1, Delta y = y2-y1.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the distance between two given points and/or the midpoint of the segment joining them
question_archetypes.example: Find the distance between (-1,4) and (3,-2), and the midpoint of the segment joining them
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two labeled points and a request for 'distance' and/or 'midpoint'
method_plan: Substitute coordinates into the distance formula and simplify the radical
Substitute coordinates into the midpoint formula
Simplify both answers fully
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct distance, radical simplified
A1: correct midpoint

common_errors.description: Sign error subtracting coordinates, especially with negative values
Leaving the radical unsimplified when it could be reduced

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given three points, use the distance formula to classify the triangle they form (right, isosceles, equilateral, or none of these)
question_archetypes.example: Show that the triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (4,3) is a right triangle
question_archetypes.answer: Side lengths 4, 3, 5; since 3^2+4^2=5^2, it is a right triangle (converse of Pythagorean theorem)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three points given with a request to classify or prove a property of the triangle they form
method_plan: Compute all three side lengths using the distance formula
Compare side lengths for equality (isosceles/equilateral) or apply the converse Pythagorean test (a^2+b^2=c^2) for a right angle
State the conclusion with justification
full_mark_rubric: M1: all three distances computed correctly
A1: correct classification with the relevant numeric check shown
A1: clearly stated conclusion

common_errors.description: Only checking two of the three side pairs before concluding
Not explicitly stating which theorem/converse justifies the classification

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the set of points equidistant from two given points, or satisfying a distance condition (introducing the perpendicular bisector or a circle)
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the set of points equidistant from (1,2) and (5,-2)
question_archetypes.answer: x - y = 3 (the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The phrase 'equidistant from' or 'distance from P equals distance from Q' appears
method_plan: Set the distance formula from an arbitrary point (x,y) to each given point equal
Square both sides to remove the radicals
Expand and simplify to the equation of the locus
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up the equal-distance equation
M1: correctly squares and expands both sides
A1: correctly simplified final equation

common_errors.description: Expansion error squaring a binomial
Not recognizing the resulting locus as the perpendicular bisector, missing a sanity check

micro_skills.micro_skill: Slope and equations of lines
definitions: Slope m = Delta y / Delta x = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1), the same for any two points on a nonvertical line. Vertical lines have undefined slope (not slope 0).
formulas: General linear equation: Ax + By = C
m = tan(phi) where phi is the line's inclination

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the equation of the line through two given points
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the line through (1,-1) and (3,5)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two coordinate pairs given, asked for 'the equation of the line'
method_plan: Compute the slope m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1)
Substitute m and one point into point-slope form
Simplify to slope-intercept (or requested) form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct slope
M1: correct point-slope setup
A1: correctly simplified final equation

common_errors.description: Reversing the order in Delta y or Delta x (using x2-x1 over y2-y1)
Distribution error simplifying m(x-x1)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a line in general form Ax+By=C, find its slope and x- and y-intercepts
question_archetypes.example: Find the slope and intercepts of 8x+5y=20
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Equation given in the form Ax+By=C rather than already solved for y
method_plan: Solve the equation for y to get slope-intercept form
Read off the slope and y-intercept directly
Set y=0 and solve for x to find the x-intercept
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly solves for y
A1: correct slope and y-intercept
A1: correct x-intercept

common_errors.description: Sign error dividing by B when isolating y
Forgetting to also find the x-intercept when asked for 'intercepts' (plural)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a slope and one point, find the equation of the line
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the line with slope -2 through (3,1)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A numeric slope value and a single point are both given explicitly
method_plan: Substitute the slope and point directly into point-slope form
Distribute and simplify to slope-intercept form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct point-slope setup
A1: correctly simplified final equation

common_errors.description: Sign error distributing m(x-x1)
Leaving the answer in an unrequested form without simplifying

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the equation of a vertical or horizontal line through a given point, or recognize that a given line is vertical/horizontal
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the vertical line through (5,-2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two given points share the same x-coordinate (vertical) or the same y-coordinate (horizontal), or slope is explicitly 0 or undefined
method_plan: Check whether the two points (or given info) share an x-coordinate or a y-coordinate
If x-coordinates match, the line is vertical: x = (that x-value)
If y-coordinates match, the line is horizontal: y = (that y-value)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies vertical vs horizontal case
A1: correct equation

common_errors.description: Saying a vertical line has 'slope 0' instead of undefined slope
Attempting to use the slope formula and dividing by zero without recognizing the vertical case

micro_skills.micro_skill: Parallel and perpendicular lines
definitions: Two nonvertical lines are parallel iff their slopes are equal. Two nonvertical lines are perpendicular iff the product of their slopes is -1 (each slope is the negative reciprocal of the other).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether two given lines are parallel, perpendicular, or neither
question_archetypes.example: Show the lines y=2x+1 and y=-x/2+3 are perpendicular
question_archetypes.answer: Slopes 2 and -1/2 multiply to -1, so the lines are perpendicular
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two line equations given, asked to classify their relationship
method_plan: Find (or read off) the slope of each line
Compare the slopes for equality, or compute their product
State parallel if slopes equal, perpendicular if product is -1, otherwise neither
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct slope of each line
A1: correct classification with the numeric justification shown

common_errors.description: Comparing slopes for perpendicularity by checking equality instead of computing the product
Misreading the slope from a non-slope-intercept form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the equation of the line through a given point parallel to a given line
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the line through (2,-1) parallel to y=3x+5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The word 'parallel' plus a specific point not on the given line
method_plan: Read the slope of the given line
Use the same slope with the given point in point-slope form
Simplify to the requested form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the slope to use (same as given line)
A1: correct final equation

common_errors.description: Using the negative reciprocal slope (confusing with the perpendicular case)
Arithmetic slip simplifying point-slope form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the equation of the line through a given point perpendicular to a given line
question_archetypes.example: Find the equation of the line through (2,-1) perpendicular to y=(1/3)x+5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The word 'perpendicular' plus a specific point
method_plan: Read the slope of the given line
Take the negative reciprocal to get the perpendicular slope
Use point-slope form with the given point and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly computes the negative reciprocal slope
A1: correct final equation

common_errors.description: Taking the reciprocal but forgetting to negate it (or vice versa)
Using the same slope as the given line (confusing with the parallel case)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Circles via completing the square
definitions: A circle with centre (h,k) and radius a>=0 has equation (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=a^2.
formulas: x^2+y^2+2ax+2by = c  =>  (x+a)^2+(y+b)^2 = c+a^2+b^2 (circle if RHS>0, point if =0, empty if <0)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centre and radius of a circle given in general (expanded) form
question_archetypes.example: Find the centre and radius of x^2+y^2-4x+6y=3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An equation with x^2 and y^2 terms with coefficient 1, plus linear x and y terms, set equal to a constant
method_plan: Group x-terms and y-terms separately
Complete the square for each group, adding the same constants to both sides
Rewrite in the form (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=a^2
Read off the centre (h,k) and radius a = sqrt(RHS)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completion of the square for x
M1: correct completion of the square for y
A1: correct centre
A1: correct radius

common_errors.description: Forgetting to add the completed-square constant to BOTH sides of the equation
Sign error reading off the centre coordinates (centre is (h,k) with (x-h)^2, so a +2ax term gives h=-a, not +a)
Forgetting to take the square root to get the radius (leaving radius^2 as the answer)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Write the equation of a circle given its centre and radius, or its centre and a point on the circle
question_archetypes.example: Write the equation of the circle with centre (-1,2) passing through (3,5)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Centre is given explicitly, and either a radius or a point on the circle is given
method_plan: If only a point is given, compute the radius as the distance from the centre to that point
Substitute centre and radius into (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=a^2
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius (via distance formula, if needed)
A1: correct final equation

common_errors.description: Sign error writing (x-h) when h is negative
Forgetting to square the radius on the right-hand side

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether a given general quadratic equation represents a genuine circle, a single point, or no graph at all (empty set)
question_archetypes.example: Describe the graph of x^2+y^2-2x+4y+10=0
question_archetypes.answer: Completing the square gives (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=-5; since the RHS is negative, there is no graph (empty set)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: After completing the square, the constant on the right-hand side needs to be checked for sign rather than assumed positive
method_plan: Complete the square in x and y as usual
Examine the sign of the resulting constant on the right-hand side
Conclude: positive gives a circle, zero gives a single point, negative gives the empty set
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completion of the square
A1: correct identification of the sign of the RHS and correct conclusion

common_errors.description: Assuming every completed-square equation of this form must be a circle without checking the sign
Arithmetic slip computing the final constant

micro_skills.micro_skill: Parabolas: vertex form and focus/directrix
definitions: A parabola is the locus of points equidistant from a fixed focus F and a fixed directrix line L.
formulas: x^2=4py: vertex origin, focus (0,p), directrix y=-p
y^2=4px: vertex origin, focus (p,0), directrix x=-p
y=ax^2+bx+c = a(x-h)^2+k after completing the square, vertex (h,k)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the vertex, axis of symmetry, and direction of opening of a parabola y=ax^2+bx+c
question_archetypes.example: Find the vertex, axis, and direction of opening of y=2x^2-8x+3
question_archetypes.answer: Vertex (2,-5); axis x=2; opens upward since a=2>0
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A quadratic in x given in expanded form, asked for vertex/axis/opening
method_plan: Factor out the leading coefficient from the x^2 and x terms
Complete the square inside the bracket
Rewrite as y=a(x-h)^2+k and read off vertex (h,k)
State the axis x=h and direction of opening from the sign of a
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct factoring out of leading coefficient
M1: correct completion of the square
A1: correct vertex and axis
A1: correct direction of opening with justification

common_errors.description: Forgetting to multiply the completed-square constant back by the leading coefficient before combining with the outside constant
Stating opening direction without reference to the sign of a

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a parabola in standard form x^2=4py or y^2=4px (vertex at origin), find the focus and directrix
question_archetypes.example: Find the focus and directrix of x^2=12y
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Equation already in the form x^2=(constant)y or y^2=(constant)x with vertex at the origin
method_plan: Match the given equation to the standard form x^2=4py or y^2=4px
Solve for p
State the focus and directrix using the standard-form facts
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly solves for p
A1: correct focus
A1: correct directrix

common_errors.description: Confusing which axis the parabola opens along (mixing up x^2=4py with y^2=4px)
Forgetting the factor of 4 when solving for p

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Write the equation of a parabola given a description of transformations applied to a standard catalog graph
question_archetypes.example: Write the equation of the parabola obtained by shifting y=x^2 right 3 units and up 2 units
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Description references shifting/reflecting a base parabola rather than giving coefficients directly
method_plan: Start from the base equation (e.g. y=x^2)
Apply each described transformation in order (replace x with x-c for a right shift, add d for an up shift, etc.)
Write the final equation and, if requested, expand to general form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct handling of the horizontal shift
M1: correct handling of the vertical shift (or reflection, if present)
A1: correct final equation

common_errors.description: Shifting in the wrong direction (e.g. using x+c for a right shift instead of x-c)
Applying transformations in the wrong order when both a scale and a shift are present

micro_skills.micro_skill: Ellipses and hyperbolas: standard forms and key features
definitions: Ellipse (centre origin): x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1, passing through (+-a,0) and (0,+-b).
Hyperbola (centre origin): x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, two branches, asymptotes x/a = +- y/b. Also xy=1 is a rectangular hyperbola with the coordinate axes as asymptotes.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and describe an ellipse from its equation, finding a, b, and the vertices
question_archetypes.example: Identify 9x^2+16y^2=144
question_archetypes.answer: Divide by 144: x^2/16+y^2/9=1; ellipse with a=4 (major axis along x), b=3, vertices (+-4,0), (0,+-3)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both x^2 and y^2 present with the SAME sign but different (or same) positive coefficients, summing to a constant
method_plan: Divide through so the right-hand side equals 1
Identify a^2 (under x^2) and b^2 (under y^2)
Determine which axis is the major axis by comparing a^2 and b^2
State key points (vertices/co-vertices)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly normalizes the equation to RHS=1
A1: correct a and b
A1: correct identification of major axis and key points

common_errors.description: Mixing up which axis the major axis lies on (comparing a^2 under x^2 vs y^2 incorrectly)
Arithmetic slip dividing both sides by the constant

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and describe a hyperbola from its equation, finding a, b, and the asymptotes
question_archetypes.example: Identify the hyperbola x^2/9 - y^2/4 = 1 and find its asymptotes
question_archetypes.answer: a=3, b=2, two branches opening left/right, asymptotes y = +-(2/3)x
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: x^2 and y^2 terms present with OPPOSITE signs
method_plan: Normalize so the RHS equals 1
Identify a^2 and b^2 from whichever term is positive
Determine which axis the branches open along (the axis of the positive term)
State the asymptotes x/a = +- y/b, i.e. y = +-(b/a)x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies a and b
A1: correct branch direction
A1: correct asymptote equations

common_errors.description: Forgetting that a hyperbola opens along the axis of the POSITIVE squared term, not the larger denominator
Sign error deriving the asymptote slope b/a

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a general quadratic equation in x and y (with x^2 and y^2 terms and possibly linear terms), determine which conic type it represents
question_archetypes.example: Identify the conic 4x^2-9y^2-16x-18y=29 by completing the square in both variables
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A general equation with x^2, y^2, and linear x, y terms that must first be reduced by completing the square before the conic type is clear
method_plan: Complete the square separately in x and in y
Normalize so the equation matches one of the standard conic forms

Compare the signs and coefficients of the squared terms to classify: same coefficient and sign -> circle; same sign, different coefficients -> ellipse; opposite signs -> hyperbola; only one squared variable -> parabola
State the centre/vertex and defining constants
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completion of the square in x
M1: correct completion of the square in y
A1: correct classification with reasoning
A1: correct centre and key constants

common_errors.description: Classifying by the original (unsimplified) equation instead of completing the square first
Forgetting to factor out the leading coefficient before completing the square when it isn't 1
Losing track of constants moved between sides during the two separate completions

micro_skills.micro_skill: Shifting, scaling, and reflecting graphs
definitions: Replacing x with x-c shifts the graph right by c (left if c<0); replacing y with y-c shifts up by c.
Replacing x with ax (a>0) compresses horizontal distances by factor 1/a (stretches if a<1).
x -> -x reflects in the y-axis; y -> -y reflects in the x-axis; swapping x and y reflects in the line y=x.
formulas: y=f(x-c)+d: shift right c, up d

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Describe (or sketch) the graph of y=f(x-c)+d as a shift of a known base graph, and state the domain/range
question_archetypes.example: Sketch y=1+sqrt(x-4)
question_archetypes.answer: y=sqrt(x) shifted right 4 and up 1; domain [4,infinity), range [1,infinity)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A recognizable base function (sqrt, x^2, 1/x, etc.) with a horizontal x-c and/or vertical +d adjustment
method_plan: Identify the base catalog function being transformed
Identify the horizontal shift from the x-c term and vertical shift from the +d term
Adjust the base domain/range by the same shifts
Describe or sketch the resulting graph
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of base function
A1: correct shift description
A1: correct domain and range

common_errors.description: Shifting left instead of right for x-c (sign confusion: 'minus' looks like it should go left)
Forgetting to also shift the domain/range, not just the graph shape

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify which line or axis a given transformation reflects the graph in
question_archetypes.example: Describe the transformation from y=f(x) to y=-f(x), and to y=f(-x)
question_archetypes.answer: y=-f(x) reflects in the x-axis; y=f(-x) reflects in the y-axis
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A negative sign applied to the whole function (y-reflection) or to just the input x (x-reflection)
method_plan: Determine whether the negation is applied to the output (y -> -y) or the input (x -> -x)
Match to the correct reflection: output negation reflects in the x-axis, input negation reflects in the y-axis
State the reflection line explicitly
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct identification for each given transformation

common_errors.description: Swapping which reflection goes with input-negation vs output-negation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Describe the effect of replacing x with ax (horizontal scaling) on a base graph
question_archetypes.example: Describe how the graph of y=sin(2x) relates to y=sin(x)
question_archetypes.answer: Horizontal compression by factor 1/2 (period halved from 2*pi to pi)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The input variable is multiplied by a constant other than 1 inside the function
method_plan: Identify the scale factor a multiplying x
State that horizontal distances compress by 1/a if a>1 (stretch if 0<a<1)
Apply this to any relevant feature (e.g. period, key x-values) of the specific base function
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the scale factor
A1: correctly describes compression vs stretch and its numeric effect on a key feature

common_errors.description: Believing y=f(ax) stretches by a instead of compressing by 1/a
Confusing horizontal scaling of the input with vertical scaling of the output

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Describe a graph built from a catalog base function using a combination of shift, scale, and reflection in one expression
question_archetypes.example: Describe y = -2*sqrt(3-x) + 1 as a sequence of transformations of y=sqrt(x)
question_archetypes.answer: Rewrite as y = -2*sqrt(-(x-3))+1: reflect in y-axis, shift right 3 (giving sqrt(3-x)), stretch vertically by 2, reflect in x-axis, shift up 1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Multiple transformation cues appear together: a negative sign inside AND outside the function, plus a shift constant
method_plan: Rewrite the inside expression in the form f(a(x-c)) to expose the shift and any input-reflection/scaling cleanly
List the transformations in a consistent order: horizontal reflection/scaling and shift first (innermost), then vertical scaling/reflection, then vertical shift (outermost)
State domain/range changes resulting from each step where relevant
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly isolates the horizontal shift/reflection/scale inside the function
M1: correctly identifies the vertical scale/reflection/shift outside the function
A1: transformations listed in a coherent, correct order
A1: correct resulting domain/range if requested

common_errors.description: Applying transformations in a haphazard order that doesn't correctly compose (order matters when multiple horizontal transformations are combined)
Factoring the inside expression incorrectly when extracting the horizontal shift (e.g. 3-x vs -(x-3))

micro_skills.micro_skill: Finding the domain of a function given by a formula
definitions: Definition 1 (Function): a rule assigning a unique f(x) to each x in a domain D. If a function is given by a formula with no domain specified, its domain is the largest set of reals for which the formula produces a real value: exclude division by 0 and even roots of negative quantities.

theorems.name: Vertical Line Test
theorems.statement: A curve is the graph of a function iff every vertical line meets it at most once.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a rational function h(x)=P(x)/Q(x)
question_archetypes.example: Find the domain of h(x) = x/(x^2-4)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The variable appears in a denominator
method_plan: Set the denominator equal to 0 and solve
Exclude those x-values from the reals
Write the domain as a union of intervals
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly finds zeros of the denominator
A1: correct domain written as interval union

common_errors.description: Forgetting to factor the denominator fully, missing a root
Writing the excluded points instead of the actual interval-notation domain

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a function involving an even root (square root, fourth root, etc.)
question_archetypes.example: Find the domain of f(x) = sqrt(9-x^2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An even-index radical is present with a variable radicand
method_plan: Set the radicand >= 0
Solve the resulting inequality
Write the domain as an interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up radicand >= 0
A1: correct interval

common_errors.description: Using > instead of >= (excluding a valid boundary point where the radicand is exactly 0)
Sign error solving the resulting quadratic-type inequality

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a function with BOTH an even root and a denominator, requiring intersection of two restrictions
question_archetypes.example: Find the domain of f(x) = sqrt(x+2) / (x-3)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A radical and a variable denominator both appear in the same formula
method_plan: Find the restriction from the radicand (>=0)
Find the restriction from the denominator (<>0)
Intersect both restrictions
Write the resulting domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radicand restriction
M1: correct denominator restriction
A1: correctly intersected final domain

common_errors.description: Only applying one of the two restrictions (commonly forgetting the denominator once a root is present)
Using a union instead of an intersection when combining the two restrictions

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a function whose radicand or denominator restriction requires solving a nontrivial (quadratic/rational) inequality
question_archetypes.example: Find the domain of g(x) = sqrt((x-1)/(x+2))
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The radicand itself is a rational expression, so the restriction '>= 0' becomes a rational inequality needing a sign chart
method_plan: Set the radicand >= 0
Solve this as a rational inequality using a sign chart, remembering the denominator inside cannot be 0
State the final domain, making sure the denominator's zero is excluded even at a boundary that would otherwise be included
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up the radicand >= 0 condition
M1: correctly builds and reads the sign chart
A1: correct final domain with the denominator's zero properly excluded

common_errors.description: Treating this like a simple polynomial radicand and forgetting the denominator inside also restricts the domain
Including the point where the inner denominator is zero because the outer inequality was non-strict

micro_skills.micro_skill: Even and odd functions
definitions: Definition 2: f is even if f(-x)=f(x) for all x in the domain (graph symmetric about the y-axis). f is odd if f(-x)=-f(x) (graph symmetric about the origin). If 0 is in the domain of an odd function, f(0)=0.

theorems.name: Algebra of even/odd functions
theorems.statement: Sums/differences/constant multiples of even (or odd) functions stay even (or odd); a function need be neither. Product of two even or two odd functions is even; product of an even and an odd function is odd.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine algebraically whether a given function is even, odd, or neither
question_archetypes.example: Determine whether f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1 is even, odd, or neither
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A request to classify a function's symmetry type
method_plan: Compute f(-x) by substituting -x for every x
Simplify and compare to f(x) and to -f(x)
Conclude even (f(-x)=f(x)), odd (f(-x)=-f(x)), or neither
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly substitutes -x and simplifies
A1: correct comparison and conclusion clearly stated

common_errors.description: Claiming a function is even just because it 'looks symmetric' without checking f(-x) algebraically
Sign error simplifying (-x)^n for odd n

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show a function is neither even nor odd, and describe the actual axis/point of symmetry it does have (if any)
question_archetypes.example: Is g(x)=x^2-2x even, odd, or neither? Describe its symmetry
question_archetypes.answer: Neither (g(-x)=x^2+2x != g(x), != -g(x)); but g(x)=(x-1)^2-1 is symmetric about the vertical line x=1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A quadratic or other function shifted off-centre from the origin/y-axis
method_plan: Compute f(-x) and compare to f(x) and -f(x) to rule out even and odd
Rewrite the function in a form (e.g. completed square) that reveals its true axis of symmetry
State that true symmetry explicitly
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly shows f(-x) matches neither f(x) nor -f(x)
A1: correctly rewrites to reveal the true symmetry axis/point

common_errors.description: Concluding a function has no symmetry at all just because it isn't even or odd about the origin/y-axis
Not completing the square correctly when finding the true axis

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Classify the symmetry of a product or composition of known even/odd functions without full expansion, using the algebra rules
question_archetypes.example: Is f(x) = x^3 * sin(x) even, odd, or neither?
question_archetypes.answer: Even (odd function x^3 times odd function sin x gives an even function)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is built as a product, sum, or composition of recognizably even/odd building blocks
method_plan: Identify the symmetry type of each building-block factor/term
Apply the product/sum rule for even/odd combinations (even*even=even, odd*odd=even, even*odd=odd; sums preserve only if all terms share the same type)
State the conclusion, with a quick f(-x) check as verification if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the symmetry type of each factor/term
A1: correctly applies the combination rule and states the conclusion

common_errors.description: Misremembering the product rule (e.g. thinking odd*odd=odd instead of even)
Fully expanding f(-x) by brute force instead of using the faster combination rule, wasting exam time

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the fact that an odd function defined at 0 must satisfy f(0)=0 to find an unknown parameter or complete a partial description
question_archetypes.example: If f(x) = x^3 + kx is odd and f is defined at x=0, is there any constraint on k from f(0)=0? What if instead g(x)=x^2+kx+c is odd?
question_archetypes.answer: For f(x)=x^3+kx, f(0)=0 automatically for any k (no constraint from this fact alone; oddness of f itself holds for all k). For g(x)=x^2+kx+c to be odd, we need g(0)=0, forcing c=0 (necessary but not sufficient; checking g(-x)=-g(x) further forces the x^2 term's coefficient to vanish, which is impossible unless that term is removed)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A parametrized function is claimed to be odd and the problem invites using f(0)=0 as a quick necessary condition
method_plan: Recall that an odd function defined at 0 must have f(0)=0
Substitute x=0 into the given formula and set equal to 0 to get a necessary condition on any parameters
Check whether this condition is also sufficient by testing the full f(-x)=-f(x) identity
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly states/uses f(0)=0 as a necessary condition for odd functions
A1: correctly solves for the parameter constraint
A1: correctly notes whether the condition is sufficient or only necessary

common_errors.description: Treating f(0)=0 as sufficient to prove oddness rather than merely necessary
Not using this quick necessary-condition shortcut, instead doing unnecessary full algebra

micro_skills.subtopic: Combining Functions to Make New Functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Algebraic combinations of functions and their domains
definitions: Definition 3: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (f-g)(x)=f(x)-g(x), (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x), (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x) (g(x)!=0). Domain of each (except quotients) is D(f) intersect D(g); quotient domains further exclude zeros of the denominator.
formulas: D(f/g)=D(f) cap D(g) minus {zeros of g}

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of f+g, f-g, or fg given the individual domains or formulas of f and g
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=sqrt(x), g(x)=sqrt(2-x). Find the domain of f+g
question_archetypes.answer: D(f)=[0,infinity), D(g)=(-infinity,2]; domain of f+g is [0,2]
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two functions are combined by addition, subtraction, or multiplication (no division)
method_plan: Find the domain of f alone
Find the domain of g alone
Intersect the two domains
State the formula and domain of the combination
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct domain of f
M1: correct domain of g
A1: correctly intersected final domain

common_errors.description: Taking the union instead of the intersection of the two domains
Error finding one of the individual domains

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of f/g given formulas for f and g, accounting for the extra restriction from zeros of g
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=sqrt(x+1), g(x)=x-3. Find the domain of f/g
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The combination is a quotient of two functions
method_plan: Find D(f) and D(g)
Intersect them
Additionally remove any x where g(x)=0
State the final domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct D(f) cap D(g)
A1: correctly excludes the zero(s) of g
A1: correct final domain notation

common_errors.description: Forgetting the extra step of excluding zeros of the denominator function g
Miscalculating the zero of g

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an algebraic combination of two functions at a specific x-value, first checking the point lies in the combination's domain
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=x^2+1, g(x)=sqrt(x). Find (f*g)(4)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A specific numeric x-value is substituted into a named combination like (f+g)(a) or (fg)(a)
method_plan: Check the point is in the domain of the combination
Evaluate f at the point and g at the point separately
Combine according to the operation specified
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct evaluation of f at the point
M1: correct evaluation of g at the point
A1: correct final combined value

common_errors.description: Evaluating the wrong function or plugging into the combined formula incorrectly
Not checking domain validity before evaluating (usually fine numerically, but expected as a stated step)

micro_skills.subtopic: Combining Functions to Make New Functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Composite functions and their domains
definitions: Definition 4: (f o g)(x) = f(g(x)). Domain of f o g: all x in D(g) such that g(x) in D(f). g is the inner function (computed first); f is the outer function.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute a composite function f(g(x)) and simplify
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=x+5, g(x)=x^2-3. Find f(g(x)) and g(f(x))
question_archetypes.answer: f(g(x))=x^2+2; g(f(x))=x^2+10x+22; note f o g != g o f
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Notation f(g(x)) or (f o g)(x) with explicit formulas for f and g given
method_plan: Substitute the entire formula for g(x) in place of x wherever it appears in f
Simplify the resulting expression
Repeat in the other order if asked, and note whether the two composites agree
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution
A1: correctly simplified result
A1: correct second composite (if requested) with explicit non-commutativity remark

common_errors.description: Reversing the order of composition (computing g(f(x)) when f(g(x)) was asked)
Expansion error simplifying the substituted expression

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a composite function f(g(x)), combining the domain restriction of the inner function with the requirement that its output lands in the domain of the outer function
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=sqrt(x), g(x)=sqrt(1-x). Find f(g(x)) and its domain
question_archetypes.answer: f(g(x)) = (1-x)^(1/4); domain (-infinity,1] (need 1-x>=0 for g, and g(x)>=0 is automatic since it's a square root)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One or both of the inner/outer functions has a restricted domain (a root or denominator)
method_plan: Find the domain of the inner function g
Determine which x in that domain also satisfy g(x) in D(f)
Intersect these two conditions
State the final domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct domain of g alone
M1: correctly identifies the condition g(x) in D(f)
A1: correctly intersected final domain

common_errors.description: Only using D(g) and forgetting the extra condition that g(x) must lie in D(f)
Solving g(x) in D(f) incorrectly (e.g. wrong inequality direction)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the domain of a composite function whose algebraic simplification cancels or hides a restriction that must still be honoured
question_archetypes.example: G(x) = (1-x)/(1+x). Compute G(G(x)) and its domain
question_archetypes.answer: G(G(x)) simplifies to x, but the domain must still exclude x=-1 (excluded from D(G) before composing)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: After substituting and simplifying algebraically, the composite formula looks defined everywhere (or more broadly than expected)
method_plan: Determine the domain restriction(s) from the ORIGINAL (unsimplified) composite before any algebraic cancellation
Simplify the composite formula algebraically
State the domain using the restrictions found before simplifying, not the simplified formula's apparent domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the pre-simplification domain restriction(s)
M1: correctly simplifies the composite formula
A1: states the final domain using the pre-simplification restriction, explicitly noting the discrepancy

common_errors.description: Reading the domain off the simplified formula instead of the original composite, missing an excluded point
Not explaining why the excluded point must still be removed despite the simplified formula being defined there

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute a repeated self-composition f(f(x)) (or f applied n times) and describe any resulting pattern
question_archetypes.example: f(x)=1/(1-x). Find f(f(x)) and f(f(f(x)))
question_archetypes.answer: f(f(x)) = (x-1)/x; f(f(f(x))) = x (the composition cycles with period 3, excluding x=0,1 from the domain along the way)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The same function is composed with itself, possibly more than once, and the notation f^(2)(x) or 'apply f twice' is used
method_plan: Substitute f(x) into itself in place of x
Simplify algebraically
Track domain exclusions accumulated at each stage of composition
Repeat for further iterations if requested, watching for a cycling pattern
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct first self-composition
A1: correctly simplified result
A1: correct further iteration and/or domain tracking if requested

common_errors.description: Substituting into the wrong copy of the formula (mixing up which x is being replaced)
Failing to track domain exclusions introduced at intermediate composition stages

micro_skills.subtopic: Combining Functions to Make New Functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Named piecewise-defined functions (Heaviside, signum, floor, ceiling)
definitions: Heaviside (unit step) function: H(x)=1 for x>=0, 0 for x<0.
Signum function: sgn(x) = x/|x| = 1 for x>0, -1 for x<0, undefined at x=0 (odd function).
Greatest integer (floor) function floor(x): greatest integer <= x.
Least integer (ceiling) function ceil(x): smallest integer >= x.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate one of the named piecewise functions (H, sgn, floor, ceiling) at several given points
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate floor(3.7), floor(-1.2), sgn(-5), H(0)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One of the named functions (or its notation, e.g. floor brackets) appears with specific numeric inputs
method_plan: Recall the piecewise definition of the named function
Apply it directly to each input value, being careful with negative numbers for floor/ceiling
State each output
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct value for each evaluation requested

common_errors.description: Rounding instead of flooring/ceiling for negative numbers (e.g. floor(-1.2) mistaken for -1 instead of -2)
Forgetting sgn(0) and H at the boundary are special-cased and must match the given definition exactly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Describe or sketch the graph of a named piecewise function, identifying jump points and their nature
question_archetypes.example: Describe the graph of H(x) near x=0
question_archetypes.answer: H is 0 for x<0 and 1 for x>=0, so there is a jump discontinuity at x=0 of size 1, with H(0)=1 (right-continuous there)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A request to describe/sketch the graph, or identify discontinuities, of a named piecewise function
method_plan: Write out each piece and its interval of validity
Identify any values where the definition changes (the 'joints')
Describe the graph shape on each piece and the jump behavior at each joint
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly describes each piece
A1: correctly identifies the jump location and size
A1: correctly states which one-sided limit matches the function's actual value there

common_errors.description: Assuming the function is continuous because it's 'built from simple pieces'
Not stating clearly which side is included at the jump point

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Simplify or rewrite an expression that combines a named piecewise function with an ordinary algebraic expression
question_archetypes.example: Simplify x * sgn(x)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A named piecewise function is multiplied by, added to, or composed with another expression
method_plan: Split into cases according to the piecewise definition of the named function
Simplify the combined expression on each case
Recognize the resulting piecewise expression as an equivalent familiar function if one exists
Note any point where the original was undefined (e.g. x=0 for sgn) and state whether it remains excluded
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct case split
A1: correct simplification on each case
A1: correctly identifies the resulting familiar function (or states the simplified piecewise form) and any domain caveat

common_errors.description: Forgetting sgn(x) (or another named function) is undefined at its joint point, silently extending the domain
Sign error in one of the case branches

micro_skills.micro_skill: Polynomial long division and the division algorithm
definitions: Definition 5 (Polynomial): P(x)=a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0, a_n!=0 if n>0; n is the degree.
Definition 6 (Rational function): R(x)=P(x)/Q(x), Q not the zero polynomial; domain excludes zeros of Q.

theorems.name: Division Algorithm
theorems.statement: If deg A_m = m > n = deg B_n, then A_m(x)/B_n(x) = Q_{m-n}(x) + R_k(x)/B_n(x), with k<n, found by polynomial long division.

formulas: A(x) = B(x)*Q(x) + R(x), deg R < deg B

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Perform polynomial long division to write A(x)/B(x) as a quotient plus a proper-fraction remainder
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A rational expression with numerator degree greater than or equal to denominator degree
method_plan: Divide the leading term of the numerator by the leading term of the denominator to get the first quotient term
Multiply the divisor by that term and subtract from the numerator
Repeat with the new remainder until its degree is less than the divisor's
Write the final result as quotient + remainder/divisor
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct first quotient term and subtraction
M1: correct subsequent steps down to remainder of correct degree
A1: correctly written final quotient + remainder/divisor form

common_errors.description: Sign error subtracting the product back from the running remainder
Stopping division before the remainder's degree is actually less than the divisor's degree
Missing placeholder zero terms for missing powers of x, causing misalignment

micro_skills.micro_skill: The Factor Theorem and finding all roots of a polynomial

theorems.name: Theorem 1 (Factor Theorem)
theorems.statement: r is a root of P (P(r)=0) if and only if (x-r) is a factor of P(x).

theorems.name: Consequence (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra)
theorems.statement: A degree-n polynomial (n>=1) has exactly n roots counting multiplicity, allowing complex roots. Complex roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs, each with the same multiplicity.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find all roots of a cubic (or quartic) polynomial that factors nicely by grouping

question_archetypes.example: Find all roots of x^3-6x^2+11x-6, given that x=1 is a root
